bullets.text: Ownership, autonomy, and responsibility reunite decision-making with accountability for a finished outcome.
AI could reduce fragmented dependencies; Brand, Product, and Intelligence are proposed paths, not new job titles.
AI could scale an individual's creative direction without the studio's extensive execution and review machinery.
Distinctive brand judgment remains valuable despite commoditized production, though this path offers no promise of high compensation.
Adding assistants to existing software can preserve the very workflows AI makes possible to rethink.
The proposed opportunity is domain-specific intelligence that changes the work, not another familiar interface.
The author presents Harvey as replacing repetitive legal workflows while retaining senior review of AI output.
Its claimed differentiation comes from choosing a consequential domain problem, rather than polishing a generic model wrapper.
Accessible building tools shift the proposed advantage toward recognizing institutional friction and unmet workflow needs.
Product sovereignty means category ownership and economic value, not merely shipping features without engineers.
Constitutions, retrieval policies, and refusal rules become design artifacts that shape model behavior and trust.
Technically informed designers can make values, conflicting evidence, and refusal boundaries more useful and understandable.

sections.label: Shape agents and their builders' tools

bullets.text: Orchestration design sets permission, transparency, and failure behavior for agents acting on users' behalf.
Developer experience makes powerful infrastructure learnable, debuggable, and usable beyond its expert builders.
Intelligence sovereignty rests on technical credibility and working prototypes, not replacing researchers or engineers.
Success is measured in better shipped systems and expert trust, rather than portfolio visibility.
The closing relocates human-centered design from surface craft to the decisions shaping intelligent systems.
The author argues that entrenched model behaviors and crowded application markets make delayed reskilling costly.
The author leaves daily practice, portfolios, and designers' unique advantage as open questions.
Further investigation, rather than a finished playbook, is offered as the next step.

notes.text: The return to craft depends on AI shrinking coordination costs, but the definition also requires authority over decisions. Faster execution alone would not establish the sovereignty the author is describing.

If AI replaces the junior work through which craft was learned, how will a young designer test whether their distinctive lens is developing? The essay proposes AI partnership as the alternative, rather than preserving the apprenticeship ladder.
What would show that a workflow needs replacement rather than a faster tool? The opportunity depends on designers' knowledge of institutional friction, not simply access to code generation.
Here, sovereignty means becoming useful in consequential decisions, not claiming ownership of alignment or engineering. That is a narrower form of authority than the word itself might suggest.

The author explicitly leaves open whether designers have a unique advantage over anyone with a human lens. What evidence from day-to-day practice would distinguish a design-specific advantage from general AI fluency?
